checks.prompt: Two teams need speech recognition. Team A wants a transcript of a few dozen recordings on a laptop this afternoon. Team B has a GPU cluster, thousands of hours of domain audio with transcripts, and intends to fine-tune a recogniser and later deploy it for low-latency streaming. Which team should adopt this toolkit, and what is the honest cost for the other?
checks.explanation: The value proposition is the plumbing: front ends, tokenisers, several decoder families, schedulers, mixed precision, multi-device training and checkpoint handling all pre-wired, so the same configuration fine-tunes on one accelerator or many, with a first-party route to production streaming. That pays off for a team that is actually training and deploying. For someone who just wants a transcript on a laptop it is the wrong shape — a large accelerator-first dependency tree for something a light transcription library does with one install.
options: Team B. The toolkit pre-wires the fiddly pieces — audio front end, tokeniser, decoders, schedulers, mixed precision, multi-device sharding, checkpoint plumbing — behind a model class, so fine-tuning is a configuration file and a training call that scales from one device to many unchanged, and there is a first-party path to production streaming deployment. Team A should not: it is heavyweight and accelerator-first, and a lighter transcription library gives them a transcript with one install
Team A. Its one-line pretrained loading is its main value, while fine-tuning at scale requires writing custom training loops that the toolkit does not provide
Both. The dependency footprint is small, so there is no cost to using it for a one-off transcript, and it is the fastest path in either case
Neither. It is a deployment server rather than a training framework, so both teams need a separate library to build or run models

checks.prompt: Describe this toolkit with the 'a high-level modelling library, opinionated toward one hardware vendor' analogy. Say what a model object bundles, what the checkpoint file actually is and why that matters, and what the data interface is. Then trace the end-to-end workflow in one sentence and say which parts you write and which the framework owns.
checks.expected: A correct answer must describe the model object as a self-contained unit bundling several things that would otherwise be assembled by hand: the audio front end that converts waveforms into spectral features, the encoder, the decoder together with its loss, and the tokeniser or vocabulary — all as a subclass of the underlying training framework's module type, so it can be trained directly. The checkpoint must be described accurately: it is a tarball containing the configuration, the weights and the tokeniser together, which is what makes it self-describing and reproducible — restoring from it rebuilds the exact graph, whereas a bare weights checkpoint from the training framework does not, because there is no configuration to rebuild from and no vocabulary to decode into. The data interface must be named as a manifest of newline-delimited JSON objects, one per utterance, carrying at least the audio path, the duration and the transcript. The workflow sentence must be roughly: a manifest goes in, a model built from configuration and weights processes it, and text comes out — with a training loop supplied by the underlying framework rather than written by hand. What you write must be identified as the manifest and the configuration, with command-line overrides on the configuration tree; what the framework owns is the training loop itself, mixed precision, gradient accumulation and multi-device or multi-node distribution, so the same configuration scales without change. A strong answer notes that reproducibility therefore lives in the configuration, and that a typo in an override is a silent or confusing failure, so checking the resolved configuration matters.

checks.prompt: A team must choose a decoder family for a recogniser that will run in a live captioning product. They ask what actually differs between the non-autoregressive frame-level decoder, the transducer, and the attention encoder-decoder. Which comparison is right?
checks.explanation: The three differ in ways that matter operationally. The frame-level decoder produces one distribution per frame over the vocabulary plus a blank and is decoded by collapsing consecutive repeats and removing blanks — non-autoregressive and therefore fast. The transducer is autoregressive but is the streaming-friendly design and usually the more accurate one, with its own beam and streaming configuration. The attention encoder-decoder underlies the multitask models that do recognition and translation together. Live captioning is the transducer's home ground, and decoding code written for one family does not carry over to another.
options: The frame-level decoder emits a distribution per frame over the vocabulary plus a blank and is decoded by collapsing repeats and dropping blanks — fast and non-autoregressive, so the whole utterance decodes in parallel. The transducer is autoregressive but designed for streaming and is usually more accurate, at the cost of a more involved decoding procedure. The attention encoder-decoder is what the multitask models use, handling recognition and translation in one model. For live captioning the transducer is the natural fit, and one family's decoding code does not transfer to another
All three decode identically once the encoder has run; the difference is only in how they are trained, so any of them suits live captioning equally
The frame-level decoder is the streaming option because it is non-autoregressive; the transducer is a batch-only design and the attention model is for training only
The transducer is the fastest because it is non-autoregressive; the frame-level decoder is autoregressive and therefore unsuitable for live use

checks.prompt: Implement the data interface and the checkpoint format. Define `REQUIRED = ("audio_filepath", "duration", "text")` and `NEMO_MEMBERS = ("config.yaml", "model_weights.ckpt", "tokenizer.txt")`. Write `parse_manifest(text)` returning the list of parsed objects from newline-delimited JSON, skipping blank lines and raising `ValueError` — with a message naming the 1-based line number, counting blank lines, and the offending field — for a line that is not valid JSON, that is not an object, that is missing any required key, whose audio path is not a non-empty string, whose duration is not a number (a boolean is not) or is not positive, or whose text is not a string. Write `total_duration(entries)`. Write `make_batches(entries, batch_size)` chopping the list into consecutive groups of at most that size, raising `ValueError` for a size below one. Write `padded_cost(batch)` returning the longest duration in the batch multiplied by its length (0.0 for an empty batch), and `padding_waste(batches)` returning the summed difference between each batch's padded cost and its real total duration. Write `sort_by_duration(entries)` returning a new list ordered by duration. Write `write_nemo(config, weights, tokenizer)` returning the bytes of an uncompressed tar archive whose three members are named by `NEMO_MEMBERS`, holding the configuration text encoded, the weights bytes and the tokeniser text encoded. Write `read_nemo(blob)` returning `{"config", "weights", "tokenizer"}` from such an archive, raising `ValueError` naming every missing member when any is absent. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Two design decisions become obvious once written out. First, the duration field is not documentation — a batch is padded to its longest clip, so its cost is the longest duration times the batch size, and mixing a one-second clip with a nine-second one in every batch throws away most of the compute. Grouping similar lengths together recovers all of it here, which is exactly why bucketing by duration exists and why a wrong or missing duration is worth catching at parse time rather than discovering as an inexplicably slow run. Second, the checkpoint is a tarball for a reason: the configuration and the tokeniser travel with the weights, so restoring rebuilds the exact graph and decodes into the right vocabulary. The final refusal makes the consequence concrete — a bare weights blob is not a model, because nothing describes the graph it belongs to.
checks.test:
import io
import json
import tarfile

MANIFEST = "\n".join([
    json.dumps({"audio_filepath": "/data/utt1.wav", "duration": 1.5, "text": "hello"}),
    "",
    json.dumps({"audio_filepath": "/data/utt2.wav", "duration": 3.0,
                "text": "hello world"}),
])

entries = parse_manifest(MANIFEST)
assert len(entries) == 2, entries
assert entries[0]["text"] == "hello"
assert total_duration(entries) == 4.5
assert parse_manifest("") == []
assert parse_manifest("\n\n  \n") == []

# The manifest is the data interface, so a malformed line is caught here rather
# than failing confusingly hours into a training run -- and the error says WHERE.
bad_lines = [
    ('{"duration": 1.0, "text": "x"}', "audio_filepath"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "a.wav", "text": "x"}', "duration"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "a.wav", "duration": 1.0}', "text"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "", "duration": 1.0, "text": "x"}', "audio_filepath"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "a.wav", "duration": 0, "text": "x"}', "duration"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "a.wav", "duration": -2, "text": "x"}', "duration"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "a.wav", "duration": "1.0", "text": "x"}', "duration"),
    ('{"audio_filepath": "a.wav", "duration": 1.0, "text": 5}', "text"),
    ('not json at all', "JSON"),
    ('[1, 2, 3]', "object"),
]
for line, expected in bad_lines:
    try:
        parse_manifest(line)
    except ValueError as exc:
        assert expected in str(exc), (line, str(exc))
        assert "line 1" in str(exc), str(exc)
    else:
        raise AssertionError(f"{line!r} must be refused")
# The line number reported is the real one, blank lines included.
try:
    parse_manifest(MANIFEST + "\n" + '{"audio_filepath": "c.wav", "text": "x"}')
except ValueError as exc:
    assert "line 4" in str(exc), str(exc)
else:
    raise AssertionError("the trailing bad line must be refused")

# Why the duration field earns its place: a batch is padded to its longest clip, so
# the cost of a batch is the longest duration times the batch size.
short = {"audio_filepath": "a", "duration": 1.0, "text": "a"}
long = {"audio_filepath": "b", "duration": 9.0, "text": "b"}
assert padded_cost([short, long]) == 18.0
assert padded_cost([short, short]) == 2.0
assert padded_cost([]) == 0.0

# Mixing lengths wastes most of the compute; grouping similar lengths together
# recovers it, which is exactly what bucketing by duration is for.
mixed = [{"audio_filepath": f"u{i}", "duration": d, "text": "t"}
         for i, d in enumerate([1.0, 9.0, 1.0, 9.0])]
naive = make_batches(mixed, 2)
sorted_batches = make_batches(sort_by_duration(mixed), 2)
assert padding_waste(naive) == 16.0, padding_waste(naive)
assert padding_waste(sorted_batches) == 0.0, padding_waste(sorted_batches)
assert padding_waste(sorted_batches) < padding_waste(naive)
# Sorting changes only the grouping, never the amount of real audio.
assert total_duration(mixed) == total_duration(sort_by_duration(mixed)) == 20.0
assert sum(len(b) for b in sorted_batches) == len(mixed)

assert make_batches([], 4) == []
assert len(make_batches(mixed, 3)) == 2
assert len(make_batches(mixed, 3)[-1]) == 1
try:
    make_batches(mixed, 0)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a batch size below one must be refused")

# The checkpoint format is a tarball carrying the configuration, the weights and
# the tokeniser together -- which is what makes it self-describing.
blob = write_nemo("model:\n  sample_rate: 16000\n", b"\x00\x01weights",
                  "a\nb\nc\n")
with tarfile.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(blob), mode="r") as archive:
    assert sorted(archive.getnames()) == sorted(
        ["config.yaml", "model_weights.ckpt", "tokenizer.txt"]), archive.getnames()

restored = read_nemo(blob)
assert restored["config"] == "model:\n  sample_rate: 16000\n"
assert restored["weights"] == b"\x00\x01weights"
assert restored["tokenizer"] == "a\nb\nc\n"
assert "16000" in restored["config"]

# Weights on their own are not a restorable model: without the configuration and
# the tokeniser there is no graph to rebuild and no vocabulary to decode into.
weights_only = io.BytesIO()
with tarfile.open(fileobj=weights_only, mode="w") as archive:
    data = b"\x00\x01weights"
    info = tarfile.TarInfo("model_weights.ckpt")
    info.size = len(data)
    archive.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(data))
try:
    read_nemo(weights_only.getvalue())
except ValueError as exc:
    assert "config.yaml" in str(exc) and "tokenizer.txt" in str(exc), exc
else:
    raise AssertionError("an incomplete archive must be refused")

checks.prompt: A team hits four problems in a week: recognition output is nonsense on their own recordings; a checkpoint from an older tutorial will not load; a training override they set appears to have no effect; and a run using half-precision produces losses that become not-a-number. What is the right set of explanations?
checks.explanation: Four separate and common failures. The models expect a specific sample rate and a single channel, and feeding anything else gives garbage or a shape error rather than being corrected for you. The configuration schema genuinely changes across releases, so a checkpoint and the toolkit have to be matched in version. The configuration override system keys exactly, so a mistyped key does nothing useful and the resolved configuration is the thing to inspect. And of the two common half-precision formats, one is prone to producing not-a-number values on these losses while the other is the safe default on newer hardware.
options: Nonsense output on their own recordings is almost always an audio mismatch — these models expect single-channel audio at a specific rate, so resample and downmix first. The checkpoint failing to load is version churn: the configuration schema moves across releases, so the toolkit version must match the checkpoint's. The ineffective override is an exact-key system — a mistyped key is silently ignored or errors, so the resolved configuration should be printed and checked. And the not-a-number losses are a known hazard of one half-precision format on these losses; the other, on newer hardware, is the safer choice
All four are the same problem — an incompatible accelerator driver — and updating it resolves the audio handling, the checkpoint loading, the overrides and the numerical stability together
Nonsense output means the wrong decoder family was used; the checkpoint problem means the file was truncated; overrides only apply at inference; and half-precision losses require a smaller batch size

The audio mismatch is corrected automatically by the front end; the checkpoint issue is a licensing check; overrides need to be set as environment variables; and the numerical problem is fixed by disabling the loss entirely

checks.prompt: Compare this toolkit with a lightweight transcription library, with a general-purpose model hub library, with a friendlier research speech framework, and with writing your own training code. Say what each is best at. Then advise a media company that wants (a) same-day transcripts of an archive on the machines they already have, and (b) a fine-tuned recogniser for their in-house jargon, deployed behind a low-latency streaming service. Say what you would use for each and why.
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all four. The lightweight transcription library is far lighter, installs in one step, runs well without specialised hardware and needs no data manifest — the right answer for quick or offline transcription. The general-purpose model hub library has a broader ecosystem and a simpler interface with easy operation on ordinary hardware, though it lacks first-class multi-device training and a vendor deployment path. The friendlier research framework is more hackable with a lighter installation and suits experimentation, but does not scale as far. Writing your own gives maximum control but means re-implementing front ends, decoders, distributed training and checkpoint handling, and is only justified for a genuinely novel architecture. This toolkit is best when you are fine-tuning speech models at scale, want the vendor's strongest checkpoints, or are deploying through their inference stack. The recommendation must split the two jobs: the archive transcription should use the lightweight library, because it is a one-off batch on existing hardware and no training or manifest is involved; the fine-tuned in-house recogniser with low-latency streaming deployment is this toolkit's case, because fine-tuning on domain audio, a transducer-style streaming decoder and export to the vendor's inference server are precisely what it provides. A strong answer notes the practical prerequisites for the second job — a validated manifest with correct durations, matching the toolkit version to the checkpoint, and audio resampled to the model's expected rate and channel count — and that the two choices can coexist rather than being a single platform decision.
